- When sentiment history shows a single strong positive signal (e.g., 1.00) followed by neutral or weak sentiment, model tends to overreact and overshoot in the short term — reduce forecast peak by 5–10% after the spike.
- If recent history shows a sustained downward trend (e.g., 3+ consecutive lower prices), model often underestimates the rebound — increase forecast by 3–7% in the next 5–7 days to capture mean reversion.
- Model consistently overestimates prices in the 10–15 day horizon after a strong sentiment spike — adjust downward by 2–5% for 10–15 day forecasts following sentiment peaks.
- When sentiment is neutral or flat for 5+ days, model tends to drift toward historical mean — apply a slight upward bias (1–3%) to counteract mean reversion bias.
- In cases where true outcome shows a sharp upward move after a flat or declining trend, model often fails to anticipate — add a 2–5% upward adjustment in forecast if sentiment turns positive after 3+ consecutive neutral days.
- Avoid overfitting to recent 3–5 day highs — if model forecasts are consistently 5–10% above recent 30-day average, reduce forecast by 3–7% to align with historical volatility patterns.
